verdicts.note: The idea holds and every cited fact checks out. The plan already uses receipt time as the upper bound (line 186). Elson and Roemer (HotNets-I, 2002) argue for reconciling timestamps after the fact. Apple 35F9.1 lets elapsed time between in-app events leave the device. TrustedTime returns nothing until the device has been online since boot. A record stays unverifiable only if there is a reboot before it (or no valid certificate) AND another reboot before it is sent, as F1 says. The defect: the age is measured at send time, after the record was signed, so as written it travels outside any device signature. On iPhone a student can fully trust a root certificate they installed themselves (Apple support 102390) and edit the send request through a proxy. A larger age moves the computed record time earlier. That works in exactly the case F1 targets (a reboot before the record, so no forward anchor contradicts it), and it would turn a capped 'saat doğrulanamadı' record into a verified one. Dropping TrustedTime is sound only with this fix. Android's platform alternative, SystemClock.currentNetworkTimeClock (API 33), is documented as not for security use, so it does not replace TrustedTime either.

verdicts.note: Every cited fact holds in the threads. kern.boottime changes on restart and on user time changes (Oct 2018). Quinn recommends a POSIX semaphore opened with O_CREAT | O_EXCL and named '<app group ID>/<name>' (May 2023), and his footnote calls kern.boottime 'a source of entropy'. DTS confirmed kern.bootsessionuuid is gone in iOS 18 and 'was never considered API' (Feb 2025). DTS says systemUptime is not reliable for restart detection (Dec 2025). DTS says CPU-counter clocks have no specified start value at boot (Jul 2026), and that reply links the same 2023 answer. Two refinements. First, semaphore cleanup on restart is DTS's 'reasonable assumption', not a documented guarantee. Second, Apple's App Groups entitlement page now documents the '<group identifier>/<unique name>' format with a PSEMNAMLEN length cap, and EAS documents automatic App Group registration, so the setup is config only, as F2 says.

verdicts.note: The Shell package holds WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS. Settings.Global is read-only for apps. Current AOSP policy lets every domain read proc_random, and the kernel defines boot_id as fixed after the first read in each boot. I also checked the Android 7 floor: in android-7.0.0_r1, /proc/sys/kernel/random carries the generic proc label and untrusted_app has 'allow untrusted_app proc:file r_file_perms;', so in AOSP apps can read boot_id from API 24 up. The exact adb write path (settings put global boot_count) is inferred from the permission and was not tested, so medium confidence is right. Extra support: soft restarts (Android 11 to 14) keep the kernel running, so boot_id and elapsedRealtime stay continuous together. That makes boot_id the exact signal for a counter reset.

verdicts.note: I redid the arithmetic. 2 s + 100e-6 x 604,800 s = 62.48 s, and 10.64 s after 1 day. The allowance passes 10 s after 80,000 s (22.2 h) and 30 s after 280,000 s (3.24 days). 23 ppm over 7 days is 13.9 s, and 50 ppm over 7 days is 30.2 s. The plan quotes at lines 243, 291 and 341 are accurate. Line 186 rejects any record dated later than its receipt, with no allowance. Line 127 has the phone try to send right at check-in, so a fast-running counter can push an honest record past its receipt time. I checked the datasheet values on the PDF itself. The 100 ppm figure is a starting value, not a proven bound (see checked_ok_disputes).

verdicts.note: Roughtime draft-19 is dated 17 March 2026, Experimental, in the RFC Editor queue, not yet an RFC. It uses Ed25519 with a DELE delegation, runs over UDP or TCP, and needs at least three servers. The draft text I fetched words that last point as 'a client needs a list of servers, a minimum of three of which are operational and not run by the same parties'. The research's quote is worded differently but says the same thing. RFC 3161 is a TSA protocol. The piggyback quote is Elson and Roemer describing Roemer's scheme. HMAC fits because only our own server verifies the certificate.

recommendation_issues.problem: As written, no signature covers the send-time age. On iPhone, a root CA the user has chosen to trust lets a proxy enlarge the age and move the record time earlier, and this happens exactly when no forward anchor exists. The age must be signed with each send package (see the F1 correction). Removing TrustedTime is safe only after this fix.

Three gaps. (1) It leaves out the hard limit Quinn flags: POSIX semaphore names are limited to 31 UTF-8 characters (PSEMNAMLEN), and on iOS the App Group ID must start with 'group.'. So 'group.<name>/<name>' must fit in 31 characters, or sem_open fails and reboot detection silently stops working. (2) Any sem_open error other than EEXIST must count as 'restarted', failing safe to 'saat doğrulanamadı'. (3) The semaphore is a one-shot signal. Write the new-boot mark to local storage first, or call sem_unlink if that write fails. Otherwise, a launch where storage cannot be written uses up the signal and the old anchor gets reused. That can happen because third-party app data defaults to Data Protection Class C, which cannot be accessed until the first unlock after boot.

Reading /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id is not a documented Android API, and Android has closed /proc paths to apps before (Android 10 blocked /proc/net). Rather than ranking one signal as primary, count a change in either boot_id or BOOT_COUNT as a reboot, and fall back to BOOT_COUNT alone when boot_id cannot be read.

F4 depends on F1. With only the forward anchor, any certificate older than about 22 hours already makes 'fark artı pay < 10 s' impossible. So most QR records from students who have not opened the app online that day would land in the flagged band, which works against the plan's 'İşaretlenmeden kabul en az %98' target. Adopt F4 together with F1, or keep certificates fresh (see the line 192 miss).

A hard 2 s cutoff on the certificate round trip can stop refreshes on slow campus or basement links, and also at the class-exit peak if certificates ride on send responses as F6 proposes. A safer rule: keep the certificate and use the measured round trip as the fixed part of that anchor's allowance, capped at an upper limit (for example 10 s). Roughtime handles delay this way, with a maximum the implementation chooses.

Piggybacking replaces the separate refresh only if the app always makes some request when it opens with internet. If nothing is sent or downloaded at that moment, no certificate arrives. The plan should say that opening the app with internet always triggers the incremental download, which then carries the certificate.

checked_ok_disputes.claim: 100 ppm is a safe upper bound because a standard 32.768 kHz RTC crystal is ±20 ppm at 25 °C ... roughly 60 ppm worst case between 0 and 45 °C.
checked_ok_disputes.problem: This overclaims. The datasheet covers a discrete tuning-fork crystal, not a phone's sleep clock. Phone PMICs often generate the 32 kHz sleep clock with an RC circuit instead of a crystal, and that drifts more. Apple DTS says the system carries the CPU counter across sleep on the RTC, so how accurate time is during sleep depends on the device. The arithmetic (60.48 s per week) is right, and 100 ppm is a reasonable starting value, but it is not a proven bound. The field measurement F4 proposes is required, not optional.

evidence.quote: the low frequency (e.g., 32 kHz) clock unit in a PMIC is typically an RC circuit that does not provide the accuracy of an external crystal oscillator

misses.plan_quote: Pencere ve sayaç telefonun saatine değil bu hesaplanan saate göre çalışır. Telefonun kendi saati yalnız not düşülür.
misses.finding: The computed time is an absolute instant, but the schedule is local ('pazartesi 09:00'). Turning it into instants needs a time zone, and the plan never says which one. Both iPhone and Android let the user set the time zone by hand, and JavaScript Date local methods use the device's zone. If the phone expands the schedule with the device zone, an honest student whose phone is set to another zone sees the button open and close at the wrong hours and cannot check in during the real window. An international student who keeps the home zone is one example. Meanwhile the server, which keeps UTC (line 624), rejects what the phone accepted. That breaks the 'Haksız devamsız: 0' target and the 'Telefonda kayıtlı' promise. Cheaters gain nothing only if the server re-checks the window in UTC, and the plan should say so. Türkiye has used a fixed UTC+3 since 2016, so the server can send exact instants.

misses.finding: Apps targeting Android 7.0 and up do not receive CONNECTIVITY_ACTION through a manifest receiver. Only a receiver registered while the app's context is alive gets it. So 'ağ değiştiğinde' works only while the app is running, and a closed app does not refresh when the network comes back. Certificate age therefore grows between app opens, which directly widens the allowance (62 s at 7 days, see F4). The plan already runs expo-background-task for sending (line 689) and can refresh the certificate there at no extra cost.

misses.finding: Every computed time is the server's clock plus an elapsed interval, and the receipt-time bound (line 186) also comes from the server's clock. A wrong server clock therefore shifts every record and every window decision at once. Containers do not get their own wall clock (Linux time namespaces virtualize only CLOCK_MONOTONIC and CLOCK_BOOTTIME), so the Docker Compose stack depends on the host's time sync. The plan covers a fake clock for tests (line 646) but says nothing about the production clock.

misses.recommendation_tr: Saat belgesinin doğruluğu sunucunun saatine bağlı. Sunucu makinesinin saati NTP ile eşitlenir (kaplar makinenin saatini kullanır) ve eşitleme durumu izlenir.

verdict_reason: The researcher rated no finding high severity, and none is refuted or unverifiable. F1 is CORRECTED. As written, its send-time age is unsigned and would let an iPhone user with a trusted proxy CA turn capped unverifiable records into verified ones; with a device signature on the send package it holds. The F2 and F3 recommendations need hardening: a 31-character semaphore name, fail-safe errors, writing the new-boot mark before using up the semaphore, and treating a change in either boot signal as a reboot. One checked_ok overclaim is disputed: 100 ppm is a starting value, not a proven bound. Five misses are added: one medium (the window's time zone is unspecified, which can lock out honest students whose phone zone differs) and four low. No high-severity miss remains.
